year-2-2025/term-2-year-2/phys-285/homew.content:
SLIDE 1: “Title & Motivation”
• Title: “Quantum Biological Electron Tunneling (QBET) in Living Systems”
• Motivation: Investigate how electron tunneling at the sub-nanometer scale manifests in biomolecule–nanoparticle systems.
• Why It Matters: QBET reveals real-time redox changes of cytochrome c (Cyt c), which are crucial for understanding cell-death pathways and broader biochemical processes.
[1] [2]

SLIDE 2: “Background & Theory”
• What is Quantum Tunneling?
– Electron wavefunctions can penetrate barriers “forbidden” classically, with probability decaying exponentially as barrier width increases.
• Biological Context: Cytochrome c’s oxidized (Ox.) and reduced (Red.) states are important markers in apoptosis and other metabolic processes.
• Tunneling in Biological Systems: The sub-nanometer linkers between nanoparticles and biomolecules set the stage for measuring QBET directly.
[3] [4]

SLIDE 3: “Project Setup: QBET Method”
• A/B/C Tunnel Junction:
– A = Gold Nanoparticle (GNP), B = Linker Molecule, C = Cytochrome c
• Quantized Dips in Scattering Spectra:
– ~530 nm (Ox. Cyt c), ~520 & ~550 nm (Red. Cyt c)
– Indicates electron tunneling from GNP into distinct electronic states of Cyt c.
• Plasmonic Enhancement: Local field around GNP can speed up redox transitions.
[5] [6]

SLIDE 4: “Key Observations & Data”
• Spectral Shifts in Real Time:
– Shows transition from Ox. to Red. form of Cyt c under reductants like dithionite.
• Intracellular Measurements: Cells undergoing apoptosis vs. necrosis exhibit unique, time-dependent spectral signatures.
• Reaction Rate Comparison: QBET often proceeds faster than in bulk solution, indicating possible catalytic effects.
[7] [8]

SLIDE 5: “Conclusions”
• Non-Invasive Real-Time Probe: QBET spectroscopy gives a wireless way to monitor electron transfer inside living cells.
• Apoptosis vs. Necrosis: Differences in Cyt c redox transitions enable this method to distinguish cell-death pathways.
• Broader Significance: Could be generalized to other redox-active biomolecules, offering insights into metabolic oscillations and disease states.
[9]

SLIDE 6: “Limitations”
• Exponential Decay with Barrier Width: Minor increases in linker thickness drastically reduce tunneling probability.
• Heterogeneity in Live Cells: Intracellular conditions (e.g., pH, competing redox events) can complicate data interpretation.
• Sample Preparation: Achieving uniform sub-nanometer control over barrier thickness is difficult.
• Theoretical Complexity: Multi-electron hopping and altered barrier heights may cause deviations from simple single-electron models.
[10]

SLIDE 7: “Next Steps”
• Expand to Other Biomolecules: QBET could be applied to diverse redox enzymes—NADH, FAD, etc.
• Enhanced Instrumentation: Develop advanced nanoscopy and single-particle tracking to improve resolution and signal.
• Diagnostic Applications: Investigate how QBET signals might detect early metabolic dysregulation or cell-death signatures in clinical samples.
• Refining Linker Chemistry: Employ linkers with optimized HOMO-LUMO gaps to boost tunneling efficiency.
[11]

SLIDE 8: “Short Answer Question & Answer”
Short Answer Q:
“How does QBET distinguish between apoptosis and necrosis in cells?”
Answer:
“QBET captures the evolving redox status of Cyt c through dips at ~530 nm (oxidized) and ~520/550 nm (reduced). Apoptosis produces a regulated, stepwise shift in these dips, reflecting a controlled Cyt c release. Necrosis, by contrast, is more abrupt and disorganized. Thus, the distinct dip patterns separate apoptotic from necrotic cell-death pathways.”SLIDE 1: “Title & Motivation”

KVL: Error of 0.012 % is an order of magnitude smaller than the DMM’s 0.06 % voltage accuracy.

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/exam-.content:
Lecture 1: Course Overview & Basic CPU Concepts

Abstraction layers: high-level code → assembly → machine code → microarchitecture
Processor architectures: Harvard vs. von Neumann, trade-offs in speed vs. flexibility
IC cost factors: dies per wafer, yield, cost per die formula

Lecture 2: Performance Metrics & Amdahl’s Law

CPU time breakdown: Instruction Count × CPI × Cycle Time
CPI factors: instruction mix, hardware implementation, pipeline stalls
Amdahl’s Law: overall speedup = 1/((1-f) + f/S)

Lecture 3: RISC-V ISA Fundamentals

ISA roles: defines registers, instruction formats, addressing modes
Instruction formats: R, I, S, B, U, J type field layouts
Register conventions: x0–x31, ABI names (ra, sp, t0–t6, a0–a7)

Lecture 4: Control Flow & Addressing Modes

Branches (B-type): beq, bne, blt/bltu, bge/bgeu; PC update logic
Jumps: jal (J-type) and jalr (I-type), link register behavior
Function call conventions: stack frame, prologue/epilogue, ra/sp usage
Addressing modes: register-immediate, PC-relative, U-type immediates

Lecture 5: Control Unit & ALU Control

Main Control outputs: RegWrite, MemRead/Write, MemToReg, ALUSrc, Branch, Jump, ALUOp
ALU Control input mapping: ALUOp + funct7/3 → exact ALU operation
Control signal patterns: R-type vs. load/store vs. branch vs. jump

Lecture 6: End-to-End Case Studies

Lifecycle steps: Fetch → Decode → Execute → Memory → Write-back → PC update
Case studies: R-type add, lw, sw, beq, jal walkthroughs
Control signals in action: how each signal steers datapath components

Lecture 7: Single-Cycle Datapath

5 stages in one cycle: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB
Pipeline registers: IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB in single-cycle concept
Data flow per instruction type: R/I/Store/Branch/Jump sequences
Critical path & cycle time: slowest combined stage delay

Lecture 8: Pipelining & Hazards

Pipeline benefits: overlap stages for increased throughput (ideal CPI ≈1)
Hazard types: structural, data (RAW), control hazards
Resolution techniques: forwarding, stalls/bubbles, branch prediction, flush
Performance impact: added CPI = 1 + stalls per instruction

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.content:
1. What Is an ISA?

Instruction Set Architecture (ISA): the contract between hardware and software

Defines operations, data types, registers, memory model, and binary encoding
Abstraction layers:

High-level language
Assembly language
Machine code (ISA)
Microarchitecture (implementation)






2. RISC-V Overview (RV32I)

RISC vs. CISC: simple, fixed-length instructions vs. complex variable-length
RV32I features:

32-bit instructions, registers, addresses
32 general-purpose registers: x0…x31 (x0 is hardwired to 0)
Load/store architecture (no memory-to-memory ALU)




3. 32-bit Instruction Formats
All instructions are 32 bits wide; different formats pack fields differently.















































FormatNameFieldsUse casesRRegisterfunct7 │ rs2 │ rs1 │ funct3 │ rd │ opcodeadd, sub, andIImmediateimm[11:0] │ rs1 │ funct3 │ rd │ opcodeaddi, lw, jalrSStoreimm[11:5] │ rs2 │ rs1 │ funct3 │ imm[4:0] │ opcodesw, sbBBranchimm[12] │ imm[10:5] │ rs2 │ rs1 │ funct3 │ imm[4:1] │ imm[11] │ opcodebeq, bneUUpperimm[31:12] │ rd │ opcodelui, auipcJJumpimm[20] │ imm[10:1] │ imm[11] │ imm[19:12] │ rd │ opcodejal

3.1 R-Type (Register)
| funct7 (7) │ rs2 (5) │ rs1 (5) │ funct3 (3) │ rd (5) │ opcode (7) |

Operation: rd ← rs1 OP rs2
Example:
add x5, x6, x7


3.2 I-Type (Immediate)
| imm[11:0] (12) │ rs1 (5) │ funct3 (3) │ rd (5) │ opcode (7) |

Operation: rd ← rs1 OP imm or load rd ← M[rs1 + imm]
Sign-extend imm[11] to 32 bits
Example:
addi x10, x0, 42    # x10 ← 42


3.3 S-Type (Store)
'| imm[11:5] (7) │ rs2 (5) │ rs1 (5) │ funct3 (3) │ imm[4:0] (5) │ opcode (7) |'

Operation: M[rs1 + imm] ← rs2
Immediate: concat imm[11:5]∥imm[4:0], then sign-extend


3.4 B-Type (Branch)
| imm[12] (1) │ imm[10:5] (6) │ rs2 (5) │ rs1 (5) │ funct3 (3) │ imm[4:1] (4) │ imm[11] (1) │ opcode (7) |

Branch target:
target = PC + SE(imm[12] imm[11] imm[10:5] imm[4:1] 0)
Example: beq x1, x2, offset


3.5 U-Type (Upper Immediate)
| imm[31:12] (20) │ rd (5) │ opcode (7) |

Operation: rd ← imm[31:12] << 12
Use: loading 20-bit constants (lui), PC-relative (auipc)


3.6 J-Type (Jump)
| imm[20] (1) │ imm[10:1] (10) │ imm[11] (1) │ imm[19:12] (8) │ rd (5) │ opcode (7) |

Jump target:
target = PC + SE(imm[20] imm[19:12] imm[11] imm[10:1] 0)


4. Register File & ABI Names

32 registers, each 32 bits wide
x0 is always zero
ABI names:

x1 = ra (return address)
x2 = sp (stack pointer)
x5–x7 = t0–t2 (temporaries)
x10–x17 = a0–a7 (arguments/returns)




5. Example: Assembling sw x8, 16(x9)
1. opcode = `0100011`
2. funct3 = `010` (store word)
3. rs1 = `x9` → `01001`
4. rs2 = `x8` → `01000`
5. imm = 16 → `00000010000`₂ → `imm[11:5]=0000001`, `imm[4:0]=0000`
6. Pack fields into 32 bits → machine code

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.content:
1. Branch Instructions (B-Type)

Purpose: conditional PC updates based on register comparisons
Formats recap:
| imm[12] imm[10:5] rs2 rs1 funct3 imm[4:1] imm[11] opcode |

Common opcodes:

beq (000): branch if equal
bne (001): branch if not equal
blt (100): branch if less than (signed)
bge (101): branch if greater or equal (signed)
bltu/bgeu: unsigned variants


Target calculation:

\text{PC}_{\text{next}} =
\begin{cases}
  \text{PC} + \mathrm{SE}\bigl(\mathrm{imm}_{12\mid 10:5\mid 4:1\mid 11}\,\Vert\,0\bigr), & \text{if condition true},\\
  \text{PC} + 4,                                                                    & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}

Sign-extension: assemble imm bits then extend bit 12 across upper bits


2. Jumps (J- and I-Type)
2.1 JAL (J-Type)

Opcode: 1101111
Format:
| imm[20] imm[10:1] imm[11] imm[19:12] rd opcode |

Operation:
jal rd, offset

rd ← PC + 4
PC ← PC + SE(offset_20|19:12|11|10:1|0)



2.2 JALR (I-Type)

Opcode: 1100111, funct3 = 000
Format: I-Type
Operation:
jalr rd, rs1, imm

rd ← PC + 4
PC ← (rs1 + SE(imm)) & ~1
clears LSB for alignment




3. Function Call/Return Conventions

Call: jal ra, label or jal x1, label
Return: jalr x0, ra, 0 (jump to return address register)
Stack usage:

Save caller-saved registers onto stack
Adjust sp in prologue/epilogue


Example prologue/epilogue:
addi sp, sp, -16      # allocate stack frame
sw   ra, 12(sp)
sw   s0, 8(sp)
addi s0, sp, 16       # set frame pointer
...                   # function body
lw   ra, 12(sp)
lw   s0, 8(sp)
addi sp, sp, 16       # deallocate
jalr x0, ra, 0        # return



4. Addressing Modes

Register-immediate (base): ld/st rs1 + imm
PC-relative: used by auipc, jal, beq offsets
Immediate only: U-Type for lui loads high bits
Memory-aligned offsets: offsets in bytes, must align to data width
Examples:

lw x5, 4(x10) → x5 ← M[x10 + 4]
sw x6, -8(x2) → M[x2 – 8] ← x6




5. Linking Branches & Jumps

Static labels: assembler computes offsets
PC-relative pros: position-independent code
Hazards: control hazards in pipelines (Lecture 8)

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.content:
1. Main Control Unit

Role: Generate high-level control signals from the 7-bit opcode
Inputs: opcode[6:0]
Outputs:

RegWrite   : write enable for register file
MemRead    : enable data memory read
MemWrite   : enable data memory write
MemToReg   : selects memory data vs. ALU result for write-back
ALUSrc     : selects second ALU operand (register vs. immediate)
Branch     : indicates a branch instruction
Jump       : indicates jal or jalr
ALUOp[1:0] : high-level ALU operation code for ALU Control




2. ALU Control Unit

Role: Decode exact ALU operation from ALUOp and funct fields
Inputs:

ALUOp[1:0] from Main Control
funct7[5] and funct3[2:0] from instruction


Output: ALUCtrl[3:0] selecting operation (ADD, SUB, AND, OR, SLT, …)

2.1 ALU Control Logic Table
ALUOp | funct7 | funct3 | Operation
------|--------|--------|----------
00    | ---    | ---    | ADD       # for loads/stores
01    | ---    | ---    | SUB       # for branches
10    | 0      | 000    | ADD       # R-type add
10    | 1      | 000    | SUB       # R-type sub
10    | X      | 111    | AND       # R-type and
10    | X      | 110    | OR        # R-type or
10    | X      | 010    | SLT       # set less than

3. Control Signals by Instruction Type
Type      RegWrite MemRead MemWrite MemToReg ALUSrc Branch Jump ALUOp
--------  -------- ------- -------- -------- ------ ------ ---- -----
R-type    1        0       0        0        0      0      0    10
Load      1        1       0        1        1      0      0    00
Store     0        0       1        X        1      0      0    00
Branch    0        0       0        X        0      1      0    01
JAL       1        0       0        0        0      0      1    00
JALR      1        0       0        0        1      0      1    00
X = don’t care

4. Datapath Connections

Instruction fetch → opcode → Main Control
Register operands → ALU inputs; ALUSrc selects imm for I-type
ALU result →

memory address (load/store),
branch comparand (zero flag & Branch signal)


Memory access → data memory (MemRead/MemWrite)
Write-back → MUX selects via MemToReg for register file
PC update → Jump, Branch & zero, or PC + 4


5. Example: R-Type vs Load Execution

R-type add x5, x6, x7:

Main Control: RegWrite=1, ALUSrc=0, ALUOp=10
ALU Control: funct7=0, funct3=000 → ALUCtrl=ADD
ALU computes x6 + x7, result → write-back to x5


Load lw x8, 12(x9):

Main Control: RegWrite=1, MemRead=1, MemToReg=1, ALUSrc=1, ALUOp=00
ALU Control: ALUOp=00 → ALUCtrl=ADD
ALU computes address x9 + 12, memory read → write-back to x8

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.title: 6 End to End case studies
year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.content:
1. Instruction Lifecycle Overview
Every instruction in our single-cycle CPU goes through these steps:

Fetch: PC → Instruction Memory → IR (Instruction Register)
Decode & Register Read: opcode → Control Unit; rs1/rs2 → Register File
Execute / Address Calculation: ALU computes result or branch target
Memory Access: for loads/stores, Data Memory read/write
Write-Back: result (ALU or Mem) → Register File
PC Update: PC + 4, branch target, or jump target


2. Case Study: R-Type Arithmetic (add x5, x6, x7)
add x5, x6, x7

Fetch: PC=0x1000 → IR=0x00C383B3
Decode: opcode=0110011 → R-type controls (RegWrite=1, ALUSrc=0, ALUOp=10)

rs1=x6=3, rs2=x7=4


Execute: ALUOp=10, funct7=0, funct3=000 → ALUCtrl=ADD → 3 + 4 = 7
Memory: no access (MemRead=0, MemWrite=0)
Write-Back: x5 ← 7
PC Update: PC ← PC + 4 = 0x1004


3. Case Study: Load Word (lw x8, 12(x9))
lw x8, 12(x9)

Fetch: PC=0x1004 → IR=0x00C4C503
Decode: opcode=0000011 → Load controls (RegWrite=1, MemRead=1, MemToReg=1, ALUSrc=1, ALUOp=00)

rs1=x9=0x2000, imm=12


Execute: ALUOp=00 → ALUCtrl=ADD → address = 0x2000 + 12 = 0x200C
Memory: read Mem[0x200C] → 0x12345678
Write-Back: x8 ← 0x12345678
PC Update: PC ← 0x1008


4. Case Study: Store Word (sw x10, 8(x11))
sw x10, 8(x11)

Fetch: PC=0x1008 → IR=0x00A5C023
Decode: opcode=0100011 → Store controls (MemWrite=1, ALUSrc=1, ALUOp=00)

rs1=x11, rs2=x10, imm=8


Execute: ALU computes address = x11 + 8
Memory: write x10 to Mem[address]
PC Update: PC ← PC + 4 = 0x100C


5. Case Study: Conditional Branch (beq x1, x2, +12)
Assume PC=0x100C, offset=+12
beq x1, x2, label   # offset=12

Fetch: IR=0x00C10263
Decode: opcode=1100011 → Branch controls (Branch=1, ALUOp=01)

rs1=x1, rs2=x2, imm=12


Execute: ALU subtracts x1 − x2; Zero flag = (x1==x2)
PC Update: if Zero & Branch → PC = 0x100C + 12 = 0x1018
else → PC = 0x1010


6. Case Study: Jump and Link (jal x3, +16)
Assume PC=0x1010, offset=16
jal x3, 16

Fetch: IR=0x010001EF
Decode: opcode=1101111 → Jump controls (Jump=1)
Execute: calculate target = PC + 16
Write-Back: x3 ← PC + 4 = 0x1014
PC Update: PC ← 0x1020

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.title: 7 Single cycle datapath
year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.content:
1. Overview of Single-Cycle CPU

Concept: entire instruction executes in one clock cycle
Implication: cycle time must accommodate worst-case path (load/store)
Stages (all in one cycle): Fetch → Decode/Register read → Execute → Memory → Write-back → PC update


2. Datapath Components

Instruction Memory

Address = PC; outputs 32-bit instruction


Register File

Two read ports (rs1, rs2), one write port (rd)
Read data → ALU inputs or branch comparator


Sign-Extend Unit

Expands immediate fields to 32 bits


ALU

Performs arithmetic/logic based on ALU control
Inputs: rs1_data, (rs2_data or imm)


Data Memory

Address = ALU result; read/write controlled by signals


MUXes

ALU src: choose register vs. immediate
MemToReg: choose ALU result vs. memory data for write-back
PC Src: choose next PC (PC+4, branch target, jump target)


PC + 4 Adder

Computes sequential PC


Branch Adder

Computes PC + sign-extended offset




3. Control Signals (from Main & ALU Control)
Signal    | Action
----------|--------------------------------------------
RegWrite  | enables write to Register File
MemRead   | enables Data Memory read
MemWrite  | enables Data Memory write
MemToReg  | 0: ALU result → RF, 1: Data Mem → RF
ALUSrc    | 0: second ALU input = rs2, 1: = immediate
Branch    | 1: perform branch decision
Jump      | 1: use jump address
ALUOp[1:0]| selects ALU operation category

4. Data Flow per Instruction Type
R-Type (add x5,x6,x7)

Fetch instruction
Decode: rs1=x6, rs2=x7 → read register file
ALUSrc=0, ALUOp=10 → ALU computes x6 + x7
MemToReg=0, RegWrite=1 → write ALU result to x5
PC←PC+4

I-Type Load (lw x8,12(x9))

Fetch
Decode: rs1=x9, imm=12
ALUSrc=1, ALUOp=00 → ALU computes address x9+12
MemRead=1 → read Data Mem at address
MemToReg=1, RegWrite=1 → write memory data to x8
PC←PC+4

Store (sw x10,8(x11))

Fetch
Decode: rs1=x11, rs2=x10, imm=8
ALUSrc=1, ALUOp=00 → address x11+8
MemWrite=1 → store x10 to Data Mem
PC←PC+4

Branch (beq x1,x2,offset)

Fetch
Decode: rs1, rs2, offset
ALUSrc=0, ALUOp=01 → ALU computes x1 - x2 and Zero flag
If Branch=1 & Zero=1 → PC←PC+offset
else → PC←PC+4

Jump (jal x3,label)

PCSrc MUX selects jump target, writes PC+4 to x3


5. Timing Considerations

Critical path: instruction memory → control → ALU → Data Mem → register write
Single-cycle cost: cycle time = sum of component delays
Trade-off: slow cycle time vs. simpler control; motivates pipelining (Lecture 8)

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.title: 8 pipelining & data hazards
year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/in-cl.content:
1. Pipeline Basics

Goal: increase instruction throughput by overlapping stages
Classic 5-stage pipeline:

IF: Instruction Fetch
ID: Instruction Decode & Register Read
EX: Execute / Address Calculation
MEM: Data Memory Access
WB: Write-Back to Register File


Ideal speedup: ≈ 5× (one instruction completes each cycle after fill)


2. Pipeline Registers & Datapath

Between each stage, pipeline registers hold intermediate values
Registers: IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB
Data path: each stage’s inputs come from previous stage registers


3. Pipeline Hazards

Structural Hazards: resource conflicts (e.g., single memory for IF and MEM)
Data Hazards: RAW, WAR, WAW dependencies

RAW (Read After Write): true data dependency
WAR (Write After Read), WAW (Write After Write): uncommon in RISC-V single-cycle


Control Hazards: branches and jumps change PC flow


4. Data Hazard Resolution

Forwarding (Data Bypassing): feed EX/MEM or MEM/WB outputs back to ALU inputs
Stalling (Pipeline Interlock): insert bubbles (NOPs) when forwarding insufficient





















Instruction PairHazardResolutionadd x1,x2,x3sub x4,x1,x5Forward resultlw x1,0(x2)add x3,x1,x4Stall one cycle

5. Control Hazard Resolution

Flush / Squash: convert wrong-path instructions into NOPs after misprediction
Branch Prediction:

Static: always-not-taken or always-taken
Dynamic: 1-bit or 2-bit predictors, BTB


Delayed Branch (older RISC): execute fixed number of instructions before branch takes effect


6. Performance Metrics

Pipeline CPI: ideally 1, but hazards add stalls
\displaystyle \text{CPI} = 1 + \text{Stall cycles per instruction}
Speedup:
\displaystyle \text{Speedup} = \frac{\text{Single-cycle time}}{\text{Pipeline time per instruction}}


7. Example: Hazard Walkthrough
1: lw   x1,0(x2)
2: add  x3,x1,x4    # RAW hazard, use stall or forwarding
3: sub  x5,x3,x6
4: beq  x5,x0,L1    # control hazard
5: ...             # speculatively fetched
L1:
6: and  x7,x1,x8

Cycle timing diagram: show IF-IF/ID-ID/EX-EX/MEM-MEM/WB across cycles with stalls/forwards

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-254/lab/l.content:
Common Terms & Abbreviations

PC: Program Counter — holds the address of the next instruction.
R[0..31]: General-purpose registers x0–x31 (as an array processor->R).
imm: Immediate value encoded in the instruction.
funct3 / funct7: Fields in the RISC-V instruction word that further distinguish operations.
rs1, rs2: Source register indices.
rd: Destination register index.
SB-type: “S”tore / “B”ranch format.
U-type, UJ-type: Upper-immediate formats (LUI, JAL).
LENGTH_BYTE / HALF_WORD / WORD: Alignment constants for memory accesses.
sign_extend_number(x, n): Helper that sign‐extends an n-bit immediate to 32 bits.
get_branch_offset, get_store_offset, get_jump_offset: Helpers that reconstruct PC-relative offsets.


void execute_instruction(uint32_t bits, Processor *proc, Byte *mem) { … }
opcode (7 bits) decides which helper to call.

After a normal instruction, does proc->PC += 4 to fetch the next.

R-Type Instructions
void execute_rtype(Instruction instr, Processor *proc) { … }
Handles R-type (register-to-register) ops:

    funct3 = 0x0 + funct7 = 0x00 → ADD

    funct3 = 0x0 + funct7 = 0x20 → SUB

    funct3 = 0x1 → SLL (Shift Left Logical)

    …and others (SLT, XOR, SRL/SRA, OR, AND).

Updates proc->R[rd] with the result, then proc->PC += 4.

I-Type (Except Loads)
void execute_itype_except_load(Instruction instr, Processor *proc) { … }
funct3 selects:

    0x0 → ADDI (Add Immediate)

    0x1 → SLLI (Shift Left by Immediate)

    0x2 → SLTI (Set Less Than Immediate, signed)

    0x3 → SLTIU (… unsigned)

    0x4 → XORI

    0x5 → SRLI/SRAI (logical vs arithmetic right shift)

    0x6 → ORI

    0x7 → ANDI

Sign-extension: for all except shift-immediates, does

imm = sign_extend_number(instr.itype.imm, 12);

Writes result to R[rd], then PC += 4.

Branches (SB-Type)
void execute_branch(Instruction instr, Processor *proc) { … }
funct3 cases:

    0x0 → BEQ (Branch if Equal)

    0x1 → BNE (Branch if Not Equal)

    (others: BLT, BGE, …)

Uses get_branch_offset(instr) for the signed 13-bit offset.

If condition is true: PC += offset; else: PC += 4.

Loads (I-Type, funct3 = 0x0–0x5)
void execute_load(Instruction instr, Processor *proc, Byte *mem) { … }
funct3:

    0x0 → LB (Load Byte, sign-ext 8 bits)

    0x1 → LH (Load Half, sign-ext 16 bits)

    0x2 → LW (Load Word, 32 bits)

    0x4 → LBU (Load Byte Unsigned)

    0x5 → LHU (Load Half Unsigned)

Computes address = R[rs1] + sign_extend_number(imm,12).

Uses load(mem, address, LENGTH_…) + optional sign-extension.

Then PC += 4.

Stores (S-Type)
void execute_store(Instruction instr, Processor *proc, Byte *mem) { … }
funct3:

    0x0 → SB (Store Byte)

    0x1 → SH (Store Half)

    0x2 → SW (Store Word)

offset = get_store_offset(instr) builds the 12-bit immediate.

address = R[rs1] + offset, then store(mem, address, LENGTH_…, R[rs2]).

Finally PC += 4.

JAL (UJ-Type)
void execute_jal(Instruction instr, Processor *proc) { … }
UJ-type encodes a 20-bit immediate → 21-bit signed offset.

Writes proc->R[rd] = PC + 4 (return address).

Updates PC += get_jump_offset(instr).

LUI (U-Type)
void execute_lui(Instruction instr, Processor *proc) { … }
U-type: 20 most significant bits of a 32-bit constant.

Does R[rd] = instr.utype.imm << 12.

Then PC += 4.

ECALL (Trap)
void execute_ecall(Processor *proc, Byte *mem) { … }
In this lab, always prints “Exiting simulator” and exit(0).

In a full OS, would dispatch on proc->R[a7] (syscall number).

Memory Helpers
Word load(Byte *mem, Address addr, Alignment a) { … }
void store(Byte *mem, Address addr, Alignment a, Word v) { … }
Little-endian layout: low address holds LSB.

LENGTH_BYTE reads/writes 1 byte, LENGTH_HALF_WORD = 2 bytes, LENGTH_WORD = 4 bytes.

Shifts and masks assemble/disassemble multi-byte values.

\bar t \;=\; \frac{1}{17}\sum_{i=1}^{17} t_i

Median:
t_{\text{med}} = 315\text{ min} = 5{:}15\text{ pm}
Mode:
t_{\text{mode}} = 330\text{ min} = 5{:}30\text{ pm}
1 (b) Variance & standard deviation
\sigma^{2} = \frac{1}{17}\sum_{i=1}^{17}\bigl(t_i-\bar t\bigr)^2
           = 3.609\times10^{3}\;\text{min}^2
\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^{2}} = 60.07\;\text{min}\;\approx1.00\text{ h}

2 Probability of drawing a white or green ball
Total balls:
4 + 6 + 3 + 8 = 21
Favourable (white + green):
4 + 8 = 12
P(\text{white or green}) = \frac{12}{21} = \frac{4}{7}\approx0.5714

3 Distinct sums from two coins
Five coins: 0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50
There are \binom{5}{2}=10 unordered pairs ⇒ 10 unique sums:
\{0.06,\;0.11,\;0.26,\;0.51,\;0.15,\;0.30,\;0.55,\;0.35,\;0.60,\;0.75\}\,\$

4 Milled metal plate
4 (a) Nominal size and combined tolerance
Initial thickness:
1.200 \pm 0.001\;\text{in}
Material removed:
0.200 \pm 0.002\;\text{in}
Nominal result:
\mu = 1.200 - 0.200 = 1.000\;\text{in}
Combined (RSS) tolerance:
\sigma_{\text{tot}} = \sqrt{0.001^2 + 0.002^2} = 0.00224\;\text{in}
Therefore:
t = 1.000 \pm 0.0022\;\text{in}
4 (b) Probability thickness > 1.0075 in
z = \frac{1.0075 - 1.000}{0.00224} = 3.35
P(t > 1.0075) = 1 - \Phi(3.35) \approx 4.0\times10^{-4}\;(0.04\%)

5 (a) More than half succeed (X\ge4)
P = \sum_{k=4}^{6}\binom{6}{k}p^{\,k}(1-p)^{\,6-k}
  = 0.5443

Let X\implies(120,\tfrac16).

z = \frac{18.5 - 20}{4.082} = -0.368
P(X\le18) \approx \Phi(-0.368) = 0.356

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/assig.content:
ENSC 280 – Assignment 2 Solutions

1. Peanut Butter Weight – Hypothesis Test

Given:

\bar{x} = 11.92
s = 0.3
n = 36
\mu = 12
\alpha = 0.01


Assumptions: Normal distribution, use z-test

Hypotheses:

H_0: \mu = 12
H_1: \mu \ne 12 (two-tailed)

Test Statistic:
z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{11.92 - 12}{0.3/\sqrt{36}} = \frac{-0.08}{0.05} = -1.6
Critical Value (for \alpha = 0.01 two-tailed):

z_{\alpha/2} = \pm 2.576

Conclusion:

|z| = 1.6 < 2.576 \Rightarrow Fail to reject H_0
P-value: \approx 0.1096

Since p > 0.01, not significant



No evidence that the mean is different from 12 oz

2. Confidence Interval for Std Dev – Height Data

Given:

n = 16
s = 2.4
Confidence intervals for population std. dev. use chi-square



(a) 95% CI:

df = n - 1 = 15
\chi^2_{0.025} = 6.262, \chi^2_{0.975} = 27.488
Formula:

\left( \sqrt{\frac{(n - 1) s^2}{\chi^2_{0.975}}}, \sqrt{\frac{(n - 1) s^2}{\chi^2_{0.025}}} \right)
= \left( \sqrt{\frac{15 \cdot 2.4^2}{27.488}}, \sqrt{\frac{15 \cdot 2.4^2}{6.262}} \right)
= (1.79, 4.17)
(b) 99% CI:

\chi^2_{0.005} = 4.601, \chi^2_{0.995} = 30.578
Same formula → Result:

= \left( \sqrt{\frac{15 \cdot 2.4^2}{30.578}}, \sqrt{\frac{15 \cdot 2.4^2}{4.601}} \right)
= (1.63, 4.59)

3. Rope Strength Claim – t-Test

Given:

\bar{x} = 7750, s = 145, n = 6, \mu = 8000, \alpha = 0.05



Hypotheses:

H_0: \mu = 8000
H_1: \mu \ne 8000

Test Statistic:
t = \frac{7750 - 8000}{145/\sqrt{6}} = \frac{-250}{59.21} \approx -4.22
Critical value (df=5): \pm 2.571
Conclusion:

|t| > 2.571 \Rightarrow Reject H_0
Manufacturer’s claim not supported


4. Light Bulb Supplier Comparison – z-Test

Given:

n_A = n_B = 100
\bar{x}_A = 1180, s_A = 120
\bar{x}_B = 1160, s_B = 40
\alpha = 0.05



Hypotheses:

H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B
H_1: \mu_A \ne \mu_B

Test Statistic:
z = \frac{1180 - 1160}{\sqrt{\frac{120^2}{100} + \frac{40^2}{100}}}
= \frac{20}{\sqrt{144 + 16}} = \frac{20}{\sqrt{160}} \approx \frac{20}{12.65} \approx 1.58
Critical value: \pm 1.96
Conclusion:

z = 1.58 < 1.96 \Rightarrow Fail to reject H_0
No significant difference between brands


5. Cotton Shipment – Binomial Proportion Test

Given:

Past proportion p_0 = 0.4
x = 20, n = 40 → \hat{p} = 0.5
\alpha = 0.05



Hypotheses:

H_0: p = 0.4
H_1: p > 0.4

Test Statistic:
z = \frac{0.5 - 0.4}{\sqrt{\frac{0.4 \cdot 0.6}{40}}} = \frac{0.1}{\sqrt{0.006}} \approx \frac{0.1}{0.077} \approx 1.30
Critical value: z = 1.645 (one-tailed)
Conclusion:

1.3 < 1.645 \Rightarrow Fail to reject H_0
Not enough evidence for quality decline


6. Marketing Campaign Effectiveness – Proportion Difference Test

Given:

Before: p_1 = 0.20, n_1 = 200
After: p_2 = 0.27, n_2 = 300



Hypotheses:

H_0: p_1 = p_2
H_1: p_1 \ne p_2

Pooled Proportion:
p = \frac{40 + 81}{500} = \frac{121}{500} = 0.242
Test Statistic:
z = \frac{0.2 - 0.27}{\sqrt{0.242 \cdot (1 - 0.242) \cdot (\frac{1}{200} + \frac{1}{300})}} 
= \frac{-0.07}{\sqrt{0.242 \cdot 0.758 \cdot 0.0083}} \approx \frac{-0.07}{0.0397} \approx -1.76
Critical value: \pm 1.96
Conclusion:

|z| = 1.76 < 1.96 \Rightarrow Fail to reject H_0
Not enough evidence campaign was successful


7. Sample Size to Detect ±0.1 lbs Error

Given:

\sigma = 0.05
Difference to detect: \delta = 0.1
Power: 95% → z_\beta = 1.645
Significance: \alpha = 0.05 → z_\alpha = 1.645



Sample Size Formula:
n = \left( \frac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta) \cdot \sigma}{\delta} \right)^2
= \left( \frac{(1.645 + 1.645) \cdot 0.05}{0.1} \right)^2
= \left( \frac{0.1645}{0.1} \right)^2 = 2.71 \Rightarrow \boxed{3}

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/assig.title: Assignment 3
year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/assig.content:
1. Coin Toss Hypothesis Test

Given: n = 900, \alpha = 0.05, p = 0.5
Mean: \mu = np = 900 \times 0.5 = 450
Std Dev: \sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{900 \times 0.5 \times 0.5} = 15
z-critical: z_{\alpha/2} = 1.96
Acceptance region:

450 \pm 1.96(15) = [420.6, 479.4]


Conclusion: Reject H_0 if heads \le 420 or \ge 480


2. Guinea Pig Birth-Weight Test

Data: n = 27, \bar{x} = 325.4963 g, s = 198.7855 g

(a) Hypothesis Test (\alpha = 0.05)

Null: H_0: \mu = 300
Test stat:

t = \frac{325.4963 - 300}{198.7855 / \sqrt{27}} \approx 0.6665


df: n - 1 = 26, t_{0.025, 26} \approx 2.0555
Conclusion: |t| < 2.0555 → Fail to reject H_0

(b) Smallest \alpha

p-value: p = 2(1 - F_{t_{26}}(0.6665)) \approx 0.5110
Conclusion: Only reject H_0 if \alpha > 0.511

(c) 95% Confidence Interval

\bar{x} \pm t_{0.025,26} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
325.4963 \pm 2.0555 \cdot \frac{198.7855}{\sqrt{27}}
CI \approx (246.86, 404.13) g


3. Proportion of Rough Bearings

Given: n = 85, x = 10 → \hat{p} = 10/85 \approx 0.1176

(a) Test H_0: p = 0.10 vs H_1: p > 0.10

z = \frac{\hat{p} - 0.10}{\sqrt{0.10 \cdot 0.90 / 85}} \approx 1.715
z_{0.05} = 1.645 → 1.715 > 1.645 ⇒ Reject H_0
p-value \approx 0.0433

(b) Power calculation at p = 0.15

Fail region: \hat{p} \le 0.11694
Z' = \frac{0.11694 - 0.15}{\sqrt{0.15 \cdot 0.85 / 85}} \approx -0.8537
\beta = \Phi(-0.8537) \approx 0.196

(c) Sample size for 90% power at p=0.15

n \approx 362


4. Comparing Two Formulations

Given: \sigma_1^2 = 1.5, \sigma_2^2 = 1.2, n_1 = 15, \bar{x}_1 = 89.6, n_2 = 20, \bar{x}_2 = 92.5

(a) Hypothesis Test H_0: \mu_2 \le \mu_1, H_1: \mu_2 > \mu_1

z = \frac{92.5 - 89.6}{\sqrt{1.5/15 + 1.2/20}} = 7.25
z_{0.05} = 1.645 → Reject H_0
p value \approx 3 \times 10^{-13}

(b) 95% CI on \mu_2 - \mu_1

CI: 2.9 \pm 1.645(0.4) = (2.242, 3.558)

(c) Sample size for \text{error} < 1 at 95% CL

n \approx 11 per group


5. Two-sample t-test: Catalyst Yield

Catalyst 1: n_1 = 12, \bar{y}_1 = 86, s_1 = 3
Catalyst 2: n_2 = 15, \bar{y}_2 = 89, s_2 = 2

(a) Test at \alpha = 0.01

s_p^2 = \frac{11 \cdot 9 + 14 \cdot 4}{25} = 6.2, s_p = 2.49
SE = s_p \cdot \sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2} \approx 0.964
t = \frac{89 - 86}{0.964} \approx 3.112
t_{0.01, 25} = 2.492 → Reject H_0

(b) 99% CI on \mu_2 - \mu_1

CI = 3 \pm 2.787 \cdot 0.964 = (0.313, 5.687)


6. Variance Comparison (F-test)

Men: n_m = 25, s_m = 0.98; Women: n_w = 21, s_w = 1.02

(a) Hypothesis Test H_0: \sigma_m^2 = \sigma_w^2, H_1: \sigma_m^2 \ne \sigma_w^2

F = \frac{0.98^2}{1.02^2} = 0.923
df_1 = 24, df_2 = 20
Critical values: F_{0.99, 24, 20} \approx 2.54, lower \approx 0.39
0.39 < 0.923 < 2.54 → Fail to reject H_0

(b) 98% CI for \frac{\sigma_m^2}{\sigma_w^2}

CI: \left(\frac{0.923}{2.54}, 0.923 \times 2.54\right) \approx (0.36, 2.42)

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/in-cl.content:
Binomial Distribution

A discrete model for n independent Bernoulli trials (success with probability p, failure with 1-p).
Random variable X = number of successes.
Probability-mass function (PMF)
P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}\,p^{k}(1-p)^{\,n-k},\qquad k=0,1,\dots ,n.

Mean and variance
\mu=np,\qquad \sigma^{2}=np(1-p).

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/in-cl.content:
Lognormal Distribution

Some phenomena grow multiplicatively rather than additively.  If
W\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^{2}),\qquad X=\exp(W),
then X is lognormal.
PDF
f(x)=\frac{1}{x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,
\exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{(\ln x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr],\qquad x>0.

Mean and variance
\mathbb E[X]=e^{\mu+\frac12\sigma^{2}},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\bigl(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\bigr)\,e^{2\mu+\sigma^{2}}.



Gamma Distribution

The gamma function generalises the factorial:
\Gamma(r)=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{\,r-1}e^{-x}\,dx,\quad r>0,
\qquad\Gamma(r)=(r-1)\Gamma(r-1).

With shape k>0 and rate \lambda>0, the gamma PDF is
f(x)=\frac{\lambda^{k}}{\Gamma(k)}\,x^{k-1}e^{-\lambda x},\qquad x>0.

Mean and variance
\mu=\frac{k}{\lambda},\qquad \sigma^{2}=\frac{k}{\lambda^{2}}.
(For integer k the gamma reduces to an Erlang; for k=\tfrac{n}{2} and \lambda=\tfrac12 it produces the \chi^{2} distribution.)


Beta Distribution

A continuous distribution bounded on [0,1]; useful for proportions.
PDF with shape parameters \alpha>0,\;\beta>0:
f(x)=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}\,
      x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1},\qquad 0<x<1.

Tuning \alpha and \beta changes the shape:

\alpha=\beta=1 → uniform;
\alpha=\beta → symmetric about x=0.5;
\alpha<1 or \beta<1 → modes at the boundaries.


Mean and variance
\mu=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},\qquad
\sigma^{2}=\frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}(\alpha+\beta+1)}.

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/in-cl.content:
3.5 Normal Distribution and Probability
Normal (Gaussian) Distribution

A normal random variable X \sim \mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^{2}) has probability-density function (PDF)
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\;
\exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr],
\qquad -\infty<x<\infty .

Standardisation: the z-score
z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).

Cumulative-Distribution Function (CDF) of a Gaussian

The CDF gives the probability that X does not exceed a threshold:
F_X(x)=P(X\le x)=\frac12\Bigl[1+\operatorname{erf}\Bigl(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma\sqrt2}\Bigr)\Bigr],
where \operatorname{erf} is the error function.
In practice we consult the standard-normal table (or software) for P(Z\le z) and convert x\!\to\!z using the formula above.

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/in-cl.content:
Quartiles & Related Descriptive Statistics
What Are Quartiles?

Definition: Quartiles split an ordered data set into four equal parts so that 25 %, 50 %, and 75 % of observations fall below Q_1, Q_2 (median), and Q_3 respectively.
Together with the minimum and maximum, the three quartiles form the five-number summary that underpins box-and-whisker plots.

Computing Quartiles (Inclusive Method)

Quartile position:
\text{Pos}(Q_k) = (n + 1)\frac{k}{4}, \qquad k = 1,2,3
where n is the sample size; interpolate if the position is not an integer.
Most spreadsheet packages (e.g., Excel QUARTILE.INC, Google Sheets QUARTILE) and MATLAB’s quantile default to this inclusive rule.

Interquartile Range (IQR)

Equation: \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1
Measures spread while ignoring extreme tails.

Detecting Outliers (Tukey Rule)

Mild outlier fences:
Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} \quad \text{and} \quad Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}
Extreme outlier fences (optional):
Q_1 - 3\,\text{IQR}, \quad Q_3 + 3\,\text{IQR}

Box-and-Whisker Checklist

Draw a rectangular box from Q_1 to Q_3 with a vertical line at the median Q_2.
Extend whiskers to the most extreme non-outlier points; mark outliers individually beyond the 1.5 IQR fences.

Formula Sheet & When to Use It

Quartile Position (inclusive):
\text{Pos}(Q_k) = (n+1)\dfrac{k}{4}
Interquartile Range:
\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1
Outlier Fences (Tukey):
[\,Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR},\; Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}\,]
Extreme Outlier Fences:
[\,Q_1 - 3\,\text{IQR},\; Q_3 + 3\,\text{IQR}\,]
Five-Number Summary for Box Plots:
\{\min,\;Q_1,\;Q_2,\;Q_3,\;\max\}

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/in-cl.content:
Guide to Error Propagation
1  Why Quote Errors?

Every measurement has a limit (± value) that brackets where the actual value can lie:contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}.
Instrument error is set by device design (e.g.\ ruler ±0.5 mm, micrometer ±0.001 mm) and user skill:contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}.

2  Types of Error




















TypeDefinitionTypical SizeInstrument (reading)Finite resolution of the deviceSpecified by manufacturerStatisticalScatter of repeated readings (includes instrument + natural variation)Use sample standard deviation

These notes follow the worst-case (maximum) method; the same algebra works with 1 σ uncertainties if you treat σ like Δx:contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}.

3  Expressing Error

Absolute error: Y \pm \Delta y (same units).
Relative error: \displaystyle \frac{\Delta y}{Y} (dimensionless).
Percentage error: \displaystyle \frac{\Delta y}{Y}\times100\%:contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}.

Example – ruler reading: t = 6.5\,\text{mm}\ \pm 0.5\,\text{mm} gives an 8 % relative error.
4  Propagation Rules
Rule 1 Addition & Subtraction
If Z = X \pm Y with X \pm \Delta x and Y \pm \Delta y then
\boxed{\Delta z = \Delta x + \Delta y}
Example: 8.5\,\text{mm} \pm 0.6\,\text{mm} from 6.5 \pm 0.5 mm + 2.0 \pm 0.1

Subtractions use the same formula; relative error often grows (4.5 mm ± 0.6 mm → 13 %):contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}.

Rule 2 Multiplication & Division
For B = XY or C = Y/X add relative errors:
\frac{\Delta B}{B} = \frac{\Delta x}{X} + \frac{\Delta y}{Y},
\qquad
\frac{\Delta C}{C} = \frac{\Delta x}{X} + \frac{\Delta y}{Y}
Example volume: V = WHL → 17 % error from adding three relative
Rule 3 General Function G = f(X)
For small \Delta x
\boxed{\Delta G \approx \left|\frac{df}{dX}\right| \,\Delta x}
With X = 5.0 \pm 0.2 m and G=X^{10},
\Delta G = 10X^{9}\Delta x \approx 3.9\times10^{6}:contentReference[oaicite:17]{index=17}.
For multivariable G=f(X,Y,\dots) sum the partial-derivative contributions:contentReference[oaicite:19]{index=19}.
Special Cases

Compare two results: subtract and add errors (Rule 1):contentReference[oaicite:21]{index=21}.
Multiply/divide by an exact constant: scale the absolute error by that constant:contentReference[oaicite:23]{index=23}.
Trig/log functions: convert angles to radians before using Rule 3:contentReference[oaicite:25]{index=25}.

5  Confidence Levels (Assuming Gaussian Errors)

About 68 % of readings lie within \,\pm 1\Delta\,,
95 % within \,\pm 2\Delta\,,
99.7 % within \,\pm 3\Delta\,:contentReference[oaicite:27]{index=27}.

6  Reporting Guidelines

Quote one, at most two, significant figures in the error:contentReference[oaicite:29]{index=29}.
Round the measured value to the same decimal place as its error.
Use % errors when specifications are given that way (common in electronics):contentReference[oaicite:31]{index=31}.


Quick Reference Sheet






























OperationPropagation FormulaWhen to UseZ = X \pm Y\Delta z = \Delta x + \Delta yAdding lengths, masses, voltagesB = XY or C = Y/X\displaystyle \frac{\Delta B}{B} = \frac{\Delta x}{X} + \frac{\Delta y}{Y}Areas, volumes, ratiosG=f(X)$\Delta G \approxf’(X)G=f(X,Y)$\Delta G \approxf_X

Tip: Always check whether worst-case propagation is appropriate; for large datasets, root-sum-of-squares (RSS) with σ may be more realistic.

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/in-cl.content:
Function of a random variable


Consider operations on a random variable is X

this shifts/scales X

Assuming that X has a mean \mu and variance \sigma


Let c be a constant in this operation

Addition and subtraction

we define this new random variable by adding c: Y=X+c
mean and variance of Y becomes

\text{mean shifts by c: }E(Y)=E(x)+c=\mu+c
the variance does not change V(Y)=V(x)+o=\sigma^2





Multiplication and division

we define the random variable as Y=cX
mean and variance of Y becomes

mean is shifted by c E(Y)=E(cX)=c\mu
variance is scaled by c as well V(Y)=V(cX)=c^{2}\sigma^{2}

variance scales with X by c









Linear Functions of random variables


Different cases when the random variables are not independent

consider X_{1}\text{ and }X_{2} being not independent

Y=X_{1}+X_{2}

since mean is additive we know that

E(Y)=E(X_{1}+X_{2})=E(X_{1})+E(X_{2})=\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}


However since its variance and the formula is the square along the square product

V(Y)=E(Y^{2})-(E(Y))^{2}

and since we know that E(X_{1}+X_{2})=\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}











General Linear function for Dependent random variables


Generally we have n random variables X_{n}

X is actually vectors or column matrix with x values
this gives us data for all the data points
each X has its own mean \mu and variance \sigma^{2}

Consider we have n+1 constants c

Y=c_{0}+c_{1}X_{1}+c_{2}X_{2}\dots

\large \implies c_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}X_{i}


The Mean is additive so it’s just the same as before where its scaled by c
However we must consider covariance (Cov(X_{i}X_{j}))

where i < j
general variance becomes

\large V(Y)=\sigma_{y}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(c_{i}\sigma_{i})^{2}+2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j>i}[c_{i}c_{j}]Cov(X_{i}X_{j})

1.4 Measurement Error and Propagation of Errors
1.4.1 Mean and Standard Deviation of R_1 Measurements
The ten repeated measurements of the paper-resistor R_1:
R_1 = [5.586,\;5.804,\;5.809,\;5.712,\;5.998,\;5.734,\;5.645,\;5.606,\;5.708,\;5.797]\;\mathrm{M\Omega}.
From these we obtain
\mu_{R_1} = 5.740\;\mathrm{M\Omega}, 
\qquad
\sigma_{R_1} = 0.121\;\mathrm{M\Omega}.

1.4.3 Uncertainty of Direct‐Measured R_s
From §1.4.2, the directly measured series resistances have
\mu_{R_s}^{\rm direct} = 9.484\;\mathrm{M\Omega}, 
\qquad
\sigma_{R_s}^{\rm direct} = 5.362\;\mathrm{M\Omega}.
At 95 % confidence (\delta = 2\sigma),
\delta_{R_s}^{\rm direct}
=2\,\sigma_{R_s}^{\rm direct}
=2\times5.362
=10.724\;\mathrm{M\Omega}.

1.4.4 Propagated Uncertainty for R_s = R_1 + R_2
The sums R_{s,i}=R_{1,i}+R_{2,i} are:







































































iR_{1,i} (MΩ)R_{2,i} (MΩ)R_{s,i} (MΩ)15.5861.4737.05925.8041.3577.16135.8094.51210.32145.7123.2288.94055.9981.5367.53465.7340.9366.67075.64511.76217.40785.6068.05613.66295.7085.84411.552105.7971.9767.773
The individual uncertainties are
\delta_{R_1}=2\,\sigma_{R_1}=2\times0.121=0.242\;\mathrm{M\Omega},
\qquad
\delta_{R_2}=2\,\sigma_{R_2}=2\times3.557=7.113\;\mathrm{M\Omega}.
By propagation for sums,
\delta_{R_s}^{\rm prop}
=\sqrt{\delta_{R_1}^2 + \delta_{R_2}^2}
=\sqrt{0.242^2 + 7.113^2}
\approx7.117\;\mathrm{M\Omega}.

1.4.5 Comparison of Uncertainties

Direct measurement:
\delta_{R_s}^{\rm direct}\approx10.724\;\mathrm{M\Omega}
Propagation:
\delta_{R_s}^{\rm prop}\approx7.117\;\mathrm{M\Omega}
Since

\delta_{R_s}^{\rm prop}<\delta_{R_s}^{\rm direct},
the propagated uncertainty is smaller, reflecting only the known variances of R_1 and R_2 without additional series measurement.

Thermistor Behavior:
The thermistor exhibits Negative Temperature Coefficient (NTC) characteristics:

As current increases, power dissipation ((P = I^2R)) heats the device
Heating reduces resistance exponentially (Arrhenius law)
Creates positive feedback:
Higher current → More heating → Lower resistance → Further current increase


Nonlinearity Origin:
The observed nonlinear (\Delta R) vs. (I) relationship stems from:

Exponential thermal response: Resistance decays as (R \propto e^{1/T})
Power-law self-heating: Temperature rise (\Delta T \propto I^2)
Combined effect: Results in rapid resistance drop at higher currents

year-2-2025/term-3-year-2/ensc-280/probl.content:
It is vital that an area be lighted continuously


they use 3 LED bulbs with 15k hrs of lifetime

\large sd=1500\text{hrs}



only one bulb is needed to achieve sufficient lighting


with a circuit that will turn on the next bulb in line when one fails


What is theprobability it will last for 50k hrs




\begin{align}
\text{the expected mean lifetime of the lighting will be}\\
\mu_{total}=\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}+\mu_{3} =15000+15000+15000=45000 \\
\text{standard deviation}: \\
\sigma_{total}=\sqrt{ \sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}+\sigma_{3}^{2} }=2600hrs \\
\text{this doesnt give significant so} \alpha=0.05 ,\text{ie 95 conifidence} \\
\text{this is a upper tail hypothesis test} \\
H_{0}:\mu=50000\text{hrs null} \\
H_{1}: \mu<50000 \text{hrs alternate} \\
z_{1}=\frac{{x-\mu}}{\sigma}=\frac{{45000-50000}}{2600}=-1.92 \\
P(z_{1})=\frac{1}{2}\left[ 1+erf\left( -\frac{1.92}{\sqrt{ 2 }} \right) \right] =0.019 \\
\text{0.019<<}\alpha \text{ so must reject the } H_{0} \text{ hypothesis, thus only 1.9}
\end{align}

year-3-2027/term-1-year-3/ensc-316/mid-t.content:
ENSC 316 Midterm 1 Prep
The ME1 topic list from the professor’s study guide, matched to Griffiths (4th ed.) and sorted by how likely each topic is to show up. A mock midterm built from the 2017 and 2018 papers follows the map.
Exam format: 1 advanced (35 min), 2 medium (20 min each), 3 beginner (10 min each). 105 minutes total. Bring the printed formula sheet, unmodified except your name and student number.

Topic map
The percentages are the professor’s odds that a topic appears as a medium or advanced question. Start at the top.







































































OddsTopic (prof’s sub-items)GriffithsBe able to80%Path & line integrals: differential line element, work done1.3.1, 1.3.3, 1.4.1–1.4.2, 2.3.1Parameterize a curve with one parameter u, write d\vec l = \frac{d\vec r}{du}du, substitute, evaluate. Check conservative with \nabla\times\vec F.80%Scalar potential: circulation, gradient1.2.2–1.2.3, 1.2.5, 1.3.3, 1.3.5, 2.2.4, 2.3.1–2.3.2\vec E=-\nabla V in all three coordinate systems. Explain why \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec l=0 lets a potential exist.80%Surface integrals: differential area element, flux1.3.1, 1.4.1–1.4.2, 2.2.1Build d\vec a on spheres, cylinders, planes and cones. On a parameterized surface, d\vec a=(\partial_u\vec r\times\partial_t\vec r)\,du\,dt.80%Divergence theorem: Gauss’ law, integral/differential laws1.2.4, 1.3.4, 2.2.1–2.2.3Swap a flux for \int\nabla\cdot\vec F\,d\tau. Gauss’s law with a written symmetry argument, surface drawn, flux and charge computed separately.70%Coulomb’s law: convolution integral2.1.2–2.1.4, 2.3.4, (3.4.4)Set up V(\vec r_f)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\frac{\rho\,d\tau_s}{\lVert\vec r_f-\vec r_s\rVert} for lines, discs and shells. Law-of-cosines trick for a spherical shell.45%Coordinate systems: coordinate curves & surfaces, general fields1.1.4, 1.4.1–1.4.2Name the surface when one coordinate is fixed and the curve when two are. Convert unit vectors.45%Spatial integrals: regions of integration, classification of types1.3.1, 1.4Set limits on odd regions like the torus. Get d\tau from the triple product of tangent vectors.40%Metals: equilibrium properties, boundary conditions, shielding2.5.1–2.5.3, 2.3.5\vec E=0 inside, metal is equipotential, E_\perp=\sigma/\varepsilon_0. Cavity charge induces equal and opposite charge on the cavity wall. The outer surface can’t tell where it is.30%Dielectrics I: micro/macro fields, polarization4.1.1–4.1.4, 4.2.1–4.2.3Torque \vec N=\vec p\times\vec E. Bound charges \sigma_b=\vec P\cdot\hat n, \rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\vec P.30%Dielectrics II: susceptibility, permittivity, displacement4.3.1, 4.3.3, 4.4.1\vec D=\varepsilon_0\vec E+\vec P=\varepsilon\vec E, \oint\vec D\cdot d\vec a=Q_{f,enc}. Boundary conditions on D_\perp and E_\parallel.


                  
                  Skip or skim for ME1 
                  
                


1.1.5 (how vectors transform), 1.3.6, 1.6 (Helmholtz)
1.5 Dirac delta: read it once, don’t drill it
2.4 energy and 2.5.4 capacitors. Those landed on Midterm 2 and the final instead.
Ch. 3, except 3.4.4 (dipole field). You need that one for the 2017 needle question.
4.4.2–4.4.4





                  
                  Where Griffiths falls short 
                  
                

The professor parameterizes curves and surfaces with tangent vectors (d\vec T_t, d\vec T_\alpha, …) and builds d\vec a and d\tau from cross and triple products. Griffiths §1.4 only hands you the standard elements for spherical and cylindrical coordinates. For general parameterized surfaces, use the parametric surfaces section of a multivariable calc book (Stewart has one), or Notaros Ch. 1.



Notation translation
The exams don’t use Griffiths’ symbols. Keep this nearby while reading.








































MeaningYour examsGriffithsCylindrical radial coordinate\gamma, \hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}s, \hat{\mathbf s}Field point (where you measure)\vec r_f\mathbf rSource point (where the charge is)\vec r_s\mathbf r'Separation vector\vec r_{sf}=\vec r_f-\vec r_sscript r, \mathbf r-\mathbf r'Free charge densities\rho_{vg}, \rho_{sg}, \rho_{\ell g} (g = “glued”)\rho, \sigma, \lambdaVolume elementdv or d\taud\tau

Study order
Seven sessions. Each one leans on the one before it. Read the sections, then try the matching problem before opening the solution.

Coordinates and elements. 1.1.4, 1.4.1, 1.4.2. Memorize d\vec l, d\vec a, d\tau in all three systems. Drill X7.
Gradient, potential, circulation. 1.2.2–1.2.5, 1.3.3, 2.2.4, 2.3.1–2.3.2. Problems B1 and X6.
Line integrals on strange curves. 1.3.1 plus the parameterization note above. M2, then redo 2018 MT1 #4 without notes.
Flux and the divergence theorem. 1.2.4, 1.3.1 (surface part), 1.3.4. M1 and X2.
Gauss’s law and Coulomb convolution. 2.1, 2.2.1–2.2.3, 2.3.4. B3, X1, X3. Redo 2018 MT1 #5 and #6.
Metals and dipoles. 2.5.1–2.5.3, 3.4.4, 4.1.3. B2 and X4.
Dielectrics. 4.1–4.3, 4.4.1. X5, then A1 on a 35-minute timer. Finish with the whole mock midterm at 105 minutes.


What the grader wants
The 2018 sample papers still have the professor’s marking notes in the margins. Every note says some version of “show the work”:

math. A symmetry argument ends in an equation like \vec E=E_\gamma(\gamma)\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}. A sentence in English isn’t enough.
Write out the zeros. In a curl or divergence, show every component that vanishes.
Name the identities you use, e.g. \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\vec A)=0.
One operation per line in Gauss’s-law problems. Draw the Gaussian surface, define every symbol, and label which part is flux and which is enclosed charge.
Derive before you quote. C=\varepsilon S/d only counts if you derived it for that problem.
With dielectrics, find \vec D first. Gauss’s law for \vec D only needs free charge. Then \vec E=\vec D/\varepsilon.


Mock midterm
Same layout as the real exam. Each problem copies the shape of a 2017/2018 question with new numbers or geometry. Use \varepsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12} F/m and time yourself.
B1 · Electric field from a potential
Beginner · 10 min · like 2017/18 #1
a) V(\vec r_f)=x^2yz-2y^3+4xz^2. Find \vec E at \vec r_f=\hat x+\hat y+2\hat z.
b) V=\gamma^2\sin\varphi+3z (cylindrical). Find \vec E at \gamma=2,\ \varphi=\pi/6,\ z=0.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) \vec E=-\nabla V with
\nabla V=(2xyz+4z^2)\,\hat x+(x^2z-6y^2)\,\hat y+(x^2y+8xz)\,\hat z
At (1,1,2): \nabla V=20\hat x-4\hat y+17\hat z, so \boxed{\vec E=-20\hat x+4\hat y-17\hat z\ \text{V/m}}
(b) Watch the 1/\gamma on the \varphi term:
\nabla V=\frac{\partial V}{\partial\gamma}\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}+\frac1\gamma\frac{\partial V}{\partial\varphi}\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}+\frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat z=2\gamma\sin\varphi\,\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}+\gamma\cos\varphi\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}+3\hat z
At the point: \boxed{\vec E=-2\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}-\sqrt3\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}-3\hat z\ \text{V/m}}


B2 · Electrostatic shielding
Beginner · 10 min · like 2017/18 #2
A metal sphere of radius 30 cm carries net charge +2 nC. Inside it is an irregular cavity holding Q_1=+5 nC, Q_2=-1 nC and Q_3=-2 nC at unknown positions. Take V(\infty)=0. Find:
a) the total charge on the cavity wall
b) the surface charge density on the outer surface
c) the potential of the metal


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) In equilibrium \vec E=0 inside the metal. A Gaussian surface inside the metal that wraps the cavity has zero flux, so Q_{enc}=0:
q_{wall}=-(5-1-2)\ \text{nC}=-2\ \text{nC}
(b) The metal’s charge is conserved: q_{outer}=+2-(-2)=+4 nC. Cavity charges plus wall charge give zero field in the metal, so the outer surface has no idea where they sit. It spreads uniformly over the sphere:
\rho_s=\frac{4\times10^{-9}}{4\pi(0.3)^2}=3.54\ \text{nC/m}^2
(c) Outside, it looks like a 4 nC point charge at the centre:
V=\frac{q_{outer}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0R}=\frac{(8.99\times10^9)(4\times10^{-9})}{0.3}\approx 120\ \text{V}
Griffiths 2.5.1–2.5.2 (the cavity discussion)


B3 · Two charged sheets
Beginner · 10 min · like 2017 #3
Plane 1 at z=-2 cm has \rho_{sg1}=+8 nC/m². Plane 2 at z=5 cm has \rho_{sg2}=+4 nC/m². Find \vec E in all three regions.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

A single infinite sheet gives \lvert\vec E\rvert=\rho_s/(2\varepsilon_0), pointing away from positive charge on both sides (Gauss pillbox, 2.2.3). Superpose:
\frac{\rho_{s1}}{2\varepsilon_0}=451.8\ \text{V/m},\qquad\frac{\rho_{s2}}{2\varepsilon_0}=225.9\ \text{V/m}

z>5 cm: both point up, \vec E=+677.7\,\hat z V/m
-2<z<5 cm: sheet 1 up, sheet 2 down, \vec E=+225.9\,\hat z V/m
z<-2 cm: both point down, \vec E=-677.7\,\hat z V/m



M1 · Divergence theorem
Medium · 20 min · like 2018 #3
\vec F(\vec r_f)=4\gamma\,\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}+7\gamma z\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}-3z\,\hat z
a) Show the net flux out of a cube of side L doesn’t depend on where the cube sits.
b) Check the divergence theorem directly on a cylinder of radius a, 0\le z\le h, centred on the z-axis.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Every term written out:
\nabla\cdot\vec F=\frac1\gamma\frac{\partial}{\partial\gamma}(\gamma\cdot4\gamma)+\frac1\gamma\frac{\partial}{\partial\varphi}(7\gamma z)+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(-3z)=8+0-3=5
\vec F is continuously differentiable everywhere, so the divergence theorem holds for any closed volume:
\oint_S\vec F\cdot d\vec a=\int_V\nabla\cdot\vec F\,d\tau=5\int_Vd\tau=5L^3
The divergence is a constant. Only the volume matters, not the position.
(b) F_\varphi is tangent to every face and contributes nothing.

Side \gamma=a, d\vec a=a\,d\varphi\,dz\,\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}: \int_0^h\int_0^{2\pi}4a\cdot a\,d\varphi\,dz=8\pi a^2h
Top z=h, d\vec a=\gamma\,d\gamma\,d\varphi\,\hat z: (-3h)(\pi a^2)=-3\pi a^2h
Bottom z=0, d\vec a=-\gamma\,d\gamma\,d\varphi\,\hat z: F_z=0 there, so 0

Total 5\pi a^2h=5\times volume. It matches.
Griffiths 1.2.4, 1.3.4, 1.4.2


M2 · Line integral on a tilted semicircle
Medium · 20 min · like 2018 #4
Sphere S:\ x^2+y^2+z^2=A^2. Plane P:\ x-z=0 (the xy-plane rotated 45° about the y-axis). Contour C=S\cap P with x>0, from \vec r_{start}=A\hat y to \vec r_{end}=-A\hat y.
a) Define a parameter u and write the Cartesian coordinates of C.
b) Write d\vec l.
c) Evaluate \int_C\vec F_1\cdot d\vec l for the uniform field \vec F_1=F_0\hat z.
d) Evaluate \int_C\vec F_2\cdot d\vec l for \vec F_2=\frac{F_0}{A}(y\,\hat x-x\,\hat y).
e) Which field is conservative? Prove it, then confirm with a second path for \vec F_2.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) On P, z=x. Put that into S: 2x^2+y^2=A^2. With u\in[0,\pi]:
x=\tfrac{A}{\sqrt2}\sin u,\quad y=A\cos u,\quad z=\tfrac{A}{\sqrt2}\sin u
Check: u=0 gives (0,A,0), u=\pi gives (0,-A,0), and x\ge0 the whole way.
(b)
d\vec l=\frac{d\vec r}{du}du=A\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos u\,\hat x-\sin u\,\hat y+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos u\,\hat z\right)du
(c) \vec F_1\cdot d\vec l=\frac{F_0A}{\sqrt2}\cos u\,du, and \int_0^\pi\cos u\,du=0. The answer is 0, which makes sense: \vec F_1=\nabla(F_0z) and z=0 at both ends.
(d) On C, \vec F_2=F_0\left(\cos u\,\hat x-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin u\,\hat y\right):
\vec F_2\cdot d\vec l=F_0A\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos^2u+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin^2u\right)du=\frac{F_0A}{\sqrt2}du\ \Rightarrow\ \int_C=\frac{\pi F_0A}{\sqrt2}
(e) \nabla\times\vec F_1=0 since its components are constant. For \vec F_2:
\nabla\times\vec F_2=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y)\hat x+(\partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z)\hat y+(\partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)\hat z=0\,\hat x+0\,\hat y-\frac{2F_0}{A}\hat z
Not zero, so \vec F_2 isn’t conservative. Along the straight path on the y-axis (x=0), \vec F_2=\frac{F_0}{A}y\,\hat x and d\vec l=dy\,\hat y. That integral is 0. Two paths, two answers.
Griffiths 1.3.1, 1.3.3, 1.2.5


A1 · Inhomogeneous dielectric sphere
Advanced · 35 min · like 2017 #4
A sphere of radius A sits in vacuum. It’s made of a dielectric with \varepsilon_r(r)=B\,\frac{A}{r} for 0<r<A, B\ge1. A free point charge Q is at the centre. Use Gauss’s law and state every symmetry argument.
a) Find \vec D, \vec E, V for r>A.
b) Find \vec D, \vec E, V for 0<r<A.
c) Find \vec P, the bound surface charge density at r=A, and the bound volume charge density.
d) Show the total bound charge is zero.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Symmetry. The free charge is a point at the origin and \varepsilon depends only on r. Rotating about the origin changes nothing, so no component can depend on \theta or \varphi, and no tangential direction is preferred:
\vec D=D_r(r)\,\hat r
Gauss for \vec D on a sphere of radius r. It works in both regions because it only needs free charge:
\underbrace{\oint\vec D\cdot d\vec a=D_r(r)\,4\pi r^2}_{\text{flux}}=\underbrace{Q}_{Q_{f,enc}}\ \Rightarrow\ \vec D=\frac{Q}{4\pi r^2}\hat r\quad\text{for all } r
(a) r>A: \vec E=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\hat r, V=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}
(b) 0<r<A: \varepsilon=\varepsilon_0BA/r, so
\vec E=\frac{\vec D}{\varepsilon}=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0BA\,r}\hat r
V(r)=V(A)+\int_r^AE\,dr'=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0A}\left[1+\frac1B\ln\frac Ar\right]
(c)
\vec P=\vec D-\varepsilon_0\vec E=\frac{Q}{4\pi r^2}\left(1-\frac{r}{BA}\right)\hat r
\rho_{sb}(A)=\vec P\cdot\hat r\big|_{r=A}=\frac{Q}{4\pi A^2}\left(1-\frac1B\right),\qquad\rho_{vb}=-\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2P_r\right)=\frac{Q}{4\pi BA\,r^2}
(d) Bound volume charge: \int_0^A\frac{Q}{4\pi BAr^2}4\pi r^2dr=Q/B. Bound surface charge: Q(1-1/B). Near r\to0, \varepsilon_r\to\infty, and the polarization packed around Q carries -\oint\vec P\cdot d\vec a\to-Q. Sum: -Q+Q/B+Q-Q/B=0.
Cross-check: net charge inside radius r is Q-Q+Qr/(BA)=Qr/(BA). Dividing by 4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2 gives back the E from (b).
Griffiths 4.2.1, 4.3.1, 4.4.1 (the metal sphere in a dielectric shell example in 4.4.1 is close)



Extra drills
One per leftover topic, so every box on page 1 of the study guide gets a rep.
X1 · Gauss’s law, infinite charged cylinder
Medium · like 2018 #5
\rho_{vg}=\rho_0(\gamma/A)^2 for 0<\gamma\le A, zero outside, infinite along z.
a) Argue the coordinate dependence. b) Argue which components survive. c) Find \vec E inside. d) Find \vec E outside.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Translating in z or rotating in \varphi leaves the charge unchanged. Components depend on \gamma only: E_i=E_i(\gamma).
(b) The reflection z\to-z leaves the charge alone but would flip E_z, so E_z=0. Same with \varphi\to-\varphi for E_\varphi. Result: \vec E=E_\gamma(\gamma)\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}.
(c) Gaussian cylinder of radius \gamma, length L. End caps contribute nothing since \hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}\cdot\hat z=0.
\text{Flux: }E_\gamma\,2\pi\gamma L,\qquad\text{Charge: }\int_0^L\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\gamma\rho_0\frac{\gamma'^2}{A^2}\gamma'\,d\gamma'\,d\varphi\,dz=\frac{\pi\rho_0L\gamma^4}{2A^2}
\vec E=\frac{\rho_0\gamma^3}{4\varepsilon_0A^2}\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}\quad(\gamma<A)
(d) Enclosed charge stops growing at \gamma=A:
\vec E=\frac{\rho_0A^2}{4\varepsilon_0\gamma}\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}\quad(\gamma>A)
Both give \rho_0A/(4\varepsilon_0) at \gamma=A. Continuous, as it should be with no surface charge.


X2 · Total charge on a torus
Medium · like 2017 #6
Same torus as the 2017 exam: central ring radius B, tube radius A, parameters t\in(0,A), \alpha,\beta\in[0,2\pi]. This time \rho_{vg}=\rho_0(t/A)^2(1+\cos\alpha).
Find a) source coordinates, b) tangent vectors, c) d\tau, d) total charge.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) \gamma_s=B+t\cos\alpha,\quad\varphi_s=\beta,\quad z_s=t\sin\alpha, so \vec r_s=(B+t\cos\alpha)\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}(\beta)+t\sin\alpha\,\hat z
(b) Using \partial\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}/\partial\varphi=\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}:
d\vec T_t=(\cos\alpha\,\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}+\sin\alpha\,\hat z)\,dt
d\vec T_\alpha=t(-\sin\alpha\,\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}+\cos\alpha\,\hat z)\,d\alpha
d\vec T_\beta=(B+t\cos\alpha)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}\,d\beta
(c) d\tau=\lvert d\vec T_t\cdot(d\vec T_\alpha\times d\vec T_\beta)\rvert=t(B+t\cos\alpha)\,dt\,d\alpha\,d\beta
(d) Expand (1+\cos\alpha)(B+t\cos\alpha) and integrate over \alpha. Only the constant and the \cos^2\alpha term survive, leaving 2\pi B+\pi t:
Q=2\pi\frac{\rho_0}{A^2}\int_0^At^3(2\pi B+\pi t)\,dt=\pi^2\rho_0A^2\left(B+\frac{2A}{5}\right)
The real 2017 density had \cos(3\beta) in it. Since \int_0^{2\pi}\cos3\beta\,d\beta=0, the answer there is 0. That’s the “not as scary as it looks” joke.


X3 · Coulomb convolution, disc and shell
Medium · like 2018 #6
a) A disc of radius R in the xy-plane carries uniform \rho_{s0}. Write the convolution integral for V on the z-axis and evaluate it.
b) Find E_z for z>0. Check the limits R\to\infty and z\gg R.
c) A spherical shell of radius A carries uniform \rho_{s0}. Use the law of cosines to find V on the z-axis inside the shell.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) \vec r_s=\gamma_s\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}, \vec r_f=z\hat z, r_{sf}=\sqrt{\gamma_s^2+z^2}, da_s=\gamma_s\,d\gamma_s\,d\varphi_s
V(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^R\frac{\rho_{s0}\,\gamma_s\,d\gamma_s\,d\varphi_s}{\sqrt{\gamma_s^2+z^2}}=\frac{\rho_{s0}}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{z^2+R^2}-\lvert z\rvert\right)
(b)
E_z=-\frac{dV}{dz}=\frac{\rho_{s0}}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}\right)
As R\to\infty this becomes \rho_{s0}/(2\varepsilon_0), the infinite sheet. For z\gg R, \sqrt{z^2+R^2}\approx z+R^2/(2z), so V\approx\frac{\pi R^2\rho_{s0}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0z}. A point charge.
(c) r_{sf}^2=z^2+A^2-2zA\cos\theta_s. Substitute w=\cos\theta_s:
\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin\theta\,d\theta}{\sqrt{z^2+A^2-2zA\cos\theta}}=\frac{1}{zA}\Big[(z+A)-\lvert z-A\rvert\Big]
Inside (z<A) the bracket is 2z, which gives 2/A:
V=\frac{\rho_{s0}A^2\cdot2\pi}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac2A=\frac{\rho_{s0}A}{\varepsilon_0}
Constant, so no field inside. Outside the bracket is 2A, and you get the 2018 answer \rho_{s0}A^2/(\varepsilon_0z).
Griffiths 2.1.4, 2.3.4. The spherical shell example there is this exact integral.


X4 · Needle in a dipole field
Medium · like 2017 #5
+Q at (d,0,0), -Q at (-d,0,0). A tiny polarized needle at \vec r_f with \lVert\vec r_f\rVert\gg d rotates freely until it settles. Find the angle C between the needle and the x-axis. Evaluate it at \vec r_f\propto(3,0,4).


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

The needle acts as a dipole \vec p_n. Torque \vec N=\vec p_n\times\vec E is zero (and stable) when \vec p_n\parallel\vec E. So the needle lines up with \vec E.
Far field of \vec p=2Qd\,\hat x (Griffiths 3.4.4, coordinate-free form):
\vec E=\frac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}\left[3(\hat x\cdot\hat r)\hat r-\hat x\right]
Let c=\hat x\cdot\hat r=x/r. Then \vec E\cdot\hat x\propto3c^2-1 and \lvert\vec E\rvert\propto\sqrt{9c^2-6c^2+1}=\sqrt{1+3c^2}:
\cos C=\frac{3c^2-1}{\sqrt{1+3c^2}}=\frac{3x^2-r^2}{r\sqrt{r^2+3x^2}}
At (3,0,4) with r=5: \cos C=2/(5\sqrt{52})=0.0555, so C\approx86.8^\circ.
For the 2017 version (charges on the z-axis), swap x\to z.


X5 · Dielectric boundary
Beginner
Vacuum for z>0, dielectric with \varepsilon_r=3 for z<0, no free surface charge. Just above the interface, \vec E_1 points into the dielectric at 30° from the normal. Find the angle and magnitude of \vec E_2, and the bound surface charge density.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Boundary conditions: E_{1\parallel}=E_{2\parallel} and D_{1\perp}=D_{2\perp} (no free charge). So
\tan\theta_2=\varepsilon_r\tan\theta_1=3\tan30^\circ=\sqrt3\ \Rightarrow\ \theta_2=60^\circ
E_{2\parallel}=E_1/2 and E_{2\perp}=E_1\cos30^\circ/3=0.289E_1, giving \lvert\vec E_2\rvert=0.577E_1.
\vec P=\varepsilon_0(\varepsilon_r-1)\vec E_2. The dielectric’s outward normal is +\hat z and E_{2z}=-0.289E_1:
\rho_{sb}=\vec P\cdot\hat z=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\varepsilon_0E_1\approx-0.577\,\varepsilon_0E_1
Griffiths 4.3.3, 4.4.1


X6 · Conservative or not
Beginner
\vec F=(2xy+z)\hat x+x^2\hat y+x\hat z. Is it conservative? If it is, find the work from (0,0,0) to (1,2,3) without doing a line integral.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

\nabla\times\vec F=(0-0)\hat x+(1-1)\hat y+(2x-2x)\hat z=0
Curl-free everywhere, so it’s conservative. Find f with \nabla f=\vec F: f=x^2y+xz.
Work =f(1,2,3)-f(0,0,0)=2+3=\mathbf{5}. Circulation around any closed loop is 0 (Stokes).


X7 · Coordinate curves and surfaces
Beginner
a) Describe the spherical surface \theta=\pi/4, the cylindrical surface \varphi=\pi/3, and the curve \gamma=2,\ z=1.
b) Write the outward d\vec a on a sphere r=A, a cylinder \gamma=a, and the cone \theta=\theta_0.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) \theta=\pi/4 is a cone around the +z-axis with a 45° half-angle. \varphi=\pi/3 is a half-plane hinged on the z-axis. \gamma=2,\ z=1 is a circle of radius 2 in the plane z=1.
(b)

Sphere: A^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,\hat r
Cylinder: a\,d\varphi\,dz\,\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}
Cone: r\sin\theta_0\,dr\,d\varphi\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} (same geometry as the 2018 Midterm 2 capacitor)




Past-exam answer checks
Do these papers without notes first, then compare. I worked these out myself. They aren’t an official key.

Cavity shape doesn’t matter.2017 #3Sheets ±5 nC/m²\vec E=0 for z>20 cm and z<3 cm; +564.7\,\hat z V/m between2017 #4\varepsilon_r=B(A/r)^2 sphere\vec D=\frac{Q}{4\pi r^2}\hat r everywhere. Inside: \vec E=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0BA^2}\hat r (constant magnitude), V=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0A}+\frac{Q(A-r)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0BA^2}. \rho_{sb}(A)=\frac{Q}{4\pi A^2}(1-\frac1B)2017 #5Needle, dipole on z\cos C=\frac{3z^2-r^2}{r\sqrt{r^2+3z^2}}, or \tan C=\frac{3z\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{2z^2-x^2-y^2}2017 #6Torus, \cos3\beta densityQ=02018 #33\gamma\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}+6\varphi\gamma\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}+5z\hat z\nabla\cdot\vec F=6+6+5=17, flux out of unit cube =172018 #4Uniform F_0\hat x on semicirclex=A\cos u,\ y=z=\frac{A}{\sqrt2}\sin u.
